title: §.XIV [1]: With Luther vs Carolstadt/Zwingli/Tigurines — force ubiquity; refuse milder Luther/Bucer/Tigurina
pass_a_gloss: [1.] THOSE WHO WITH LUTHER — irritated partly by Carolstadt innovating many things at Wittenberg by an Authority not entirely private, partly by Zwingli writing a little more invidiously (as it could seem) and boastfully in the Explanation of his Articles at Article XVII: I began to preach the Gospel in the Year of Salvation sixteen above 1500, namely at a time when Luther's name had not even been heard in our Regions; partly finally by the Zurichers sending to Luther a translation of the Sacred Books prepared by themselves with Leo Juda as standard-bearer through the printer Forschover, after Luther desired that his own Bible Version, published especially by him, be received everywhere; (on each of which Calixtus in Judgment on Theological Controversies, nos. 48, 53, 72.) — and when those men, intending to restore to its pristine brightness the Sacrament of the Eucharist deformed among the Pontificians by many foul abuses and superstitions, seemed to have denied the presence of the Body and Blood of Christ in it — with all fervor and with a spirit pressing adversaries on every side (these are Calixtus's words, num. 47) judge that the presence of Christ's Body in the Supper must be urged so that they more importunately urge a new and inconvenient Opinion concerning Ubiquity, cut out for Luther in the heat of contests; Nor indeed do they judge that those thinking with the milder Luther and made more certain from Bucer's Declarations and the Zurich Confession — that no presence of Christ's Body in the Holy Supper was denied except the local and natural, the Sacramental and Spiritual alike being admitted — are to be borne at all as innocent and pure, easily to be freed by Christ, and they wish themselves also to be tolerated by these, although they know not how to descend into their Opinion. See the History of the Augsburg Confession composed by Kirchner, Selnecker & Chemnitz and alleged by Calixtus l. c. num. 62 at the end, compared with nums. 63, 64, 65, 69, 71, 75.
pass_b_english: [1.] Those who side with Luther against Carolstadt (innovating much at Wittenberg under authority that was not wholly private), against Zwingli (writing a little too spitefully and boastfully on Article XVII of his Articles' Explanation — "I began preaching the Gospel in A.D. 1516, when Luther's name had not even been heard in our regions"), and against the Zurichers (who sent Luther a Bible translation prepared under Leo Juda's lead and printed by Forschover, after Luther wanted his own published version received everywhere). On each of these see Calixtus, Judgment on Theological Controversies, nos. 48, 53, 72.

When those opponents, aiming to restore the Eucharist from papal abuses and superstitions to its old brightness, seemed to deny Christ's body and blood present in it, these men — "with all their heat, pressing adversaries on every side" (Calixtus, num. 47) — decide the bodily presence in the Supper must be pressed so hard that they push, too roughly, the new and awkward ubiquity opinion cut out for Luther in the heat of battle.

Nor will they bear at all those who follow the milder Luther, made surer by Bucer's Declarations and the Zurich Confession: that only a local, natural presence was denied in the Holy Supper, while sacramental and spiritual presence were both granted. Such people they will not treat as innocent and pure, easily freed by Christ; and they want tolerance from them too, though they themselves cannot come down into that milder view.
See the History of the Augsburg Confession by Kirchner, Selnecker, and Chemnitz, cited by Calixtus at num. 62 (end), with nums. 63–65, 69, 71, 75.
source_text: [1.] QUI CUM LUTHERO, partim per Carolostadium, multa Wittenbergae, non tamen omnino privatâ, innovantem Auctoritate, partim per Zwinglium, in Articulorum suorum Explanatione Articuli XVII. paulò invidiosius (ut videri poterat) atque jactantius scribentem: Capi Ego Evangelium praedicare Anno Salutis XVI. supra M.D., scilicet tempore, cùm Lutheri nomen in nostris Regionibus ne auditum quidem erat; partim denique per Tigurinos, Bibliorum Sacrorum translationem, à se, Leone Juda Antesignano, adornatam, per Forschoverum Typographum, Luthero transmittentes, postquam hic suam cumprimis Bibliorum Versionem in publicum editam, ubique recipi cuperet; (de quibus singulis Calixtus in Judicio de Controv. Theolog. nó. 48. 53. 72.) irritato, & cum isti Sacramentum Eucharistiae, multis ac tetris abusibus, & superstitionibus hactenus apud Pontificios deformatum, restituere pristino nitori intenti, praesentiam Corporis & Sangvinis Christi negasse in eo viderentur, totô fervente & undiquaque adversarios premere annisô (sunt verba Calixti num. 47.) praesentiam Corporis Christi ita in Coena urgendam arbitrantur, ut novam & incommodam de Ubiquitate Sententiam, in aestu certaminum Luthero excisam, importunius urgeant; Nec verò cum Luthero mitiori & ex Buceri Declarationibus ac Confessione Tigurina facto certiori, praesentiam Corporis Christi in S. Coena nullam, quam localem naturalemque negatam esse, Sacramentali pariter ac Spirituali admissâ, ita sentientes, omnino ferendos esse arbitrantur, tanquam innocentes & puros, à Christo facilè liberandos, seque ab his quoque tolerari optant, in suam licèt Sententiam descendere nesciis. Vid. Hist. August. Conf. à Kirchn. Selneccer. & Chemnitio confectam & Calixto allegatam l. c. num. 62. in fine, collat. cum num. 63. 64. 65. 69. 71. 75.
